palette.$description: Layer 1 primitives. Raw values only, no meaning attached. Component code never names these; it goes through the Layer 2 semantic aliases in tokens/semantic. Layer 1 is identical in every theme.

neutral.$description: Warm neutral ramp at hue ~80. Chroma stays at or below 0.015 so it reads as neutral rather than tinted, but never as the dead grey of a chroma-zero scale. Step 1 is the darkest, step 12 the lightest, in both themes; it is the semantic layer that decides which end means 'background'.

amber.$description: The one accent that carries the brand. Steps 1 to 6 are a monotonic ramp for tints, borders and text on light surfaces. The four named variants below are not ramp positions: they are the specific values the brand is defined by, and three of them sit at almost the same lightness rather than in sequence.

solid.$description: Amber at full strength: a filled button, the active state of a control. Whatever sits on top of this is palette.amber.contrast, never white. See that token.

hover.$description: Hover for a solid amber fill. Brighter than solid, not darker. On a dark UI, lifting toward the light is what reads as 'closer to the pointer'. Chroma here is past the sRGB boundary (max is ~0.161 at this lightness): it renders as written on a P3 display and clips to the gamut edge on an sRGB one. That is deliberate, and npm run tokens:check measures the clipped result, so the contrast numbers hold either way.

text.$description: Amber as a text or icon color on a dark surface. Not for light surfaces; step 3 is the light-surface equivalent. Sits a hair outside sRGB (max is ~0.174 at this lightness), which is below the threshold of visible clipping.

contrast.$description: The near-black label that goes on top of amber.solid. THIS IS NOT A BUG AND MUST NOT BE 'FIXED' TO WHITE. Amber at L 0.851 is a light color: white on it lands near 1.4:1, failing every contrast target there is, while this near-black lands near 9:1. Every design system with a light-yellow primary has to make this call, and the label is the side that gives.

teal.$description: Cool counter-accent at hue ~190. Used sparingly, and never competing with amber for the same job. Its purpose is a second, orthogonal axis of meaning, not a second brand color.

1.$description: Only light theme uses this. Teal at step 2 clears 3:1 against a dark surface but lands near 2.2:1 against a near-white one, so light needs its own step.

danger.$description: Step 1 is for light theme, step 2 for dark. A status color has to be legible as text on whatever surface it lands on, and no single lightness manages that against both a near-black and a near-white background.

success.$description: Step 1 is for light theme, step 2 for dark. See danger.

alpha.$description: Translucent hairlines. Borders use these rather than an opaque neutral so that one border value reads correctly at every surface elevation instead of needing a variant per surface.
